newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-GERMANS ACCUSE UEFA OF KOW-TOWING TO BRITISH PRESSURE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-GERMANS ACCUSE UEFA OF KOW-TOWING TO BRITISH PRESSURE.

text.p: One of the most respected voices in German soccer accused UEFA on Monday of kow-towing to British political pressure by withdrawing its unequivocal support of Germany's bid for the 2006 World Cup finals.

In a critical editorial, the football magazine Kicker, which is almost regarded as an institution in Germany, said Europe's governing soccer body had put its credibility in serious doubt by its handling of the affair.

"The way UEFA has acted in the 'England case' throws up a great deal of doubt about its credibility and seriousness," Kicker said. "This U-turn is a kow-tow, a humiliating bow to the immense pressure from British politics."
UEFA's original full backing of Germany had caused outrage in England who also want the finals.
After a meeting in London last Friday, the body withdrew its total support for Germany and agreed to meet officials from both England and Germany in April to decide which bid to back.

Kicker, which made it clear that it believed other countries in Europe had a right to bid for the finals, said UEFA's original decision to send a fax to the English authorities recently, stating its support for the Germans had been undiplomatic.

The decision by UEFA general secretary Gerhard Aigner to go to London last Friday in an effort to solve the problem after a week of mud-slinging and verbal blows was also lacking skill, the magazine said.

UEFA should have solved the problem from its headquarters in Switzerland where it could have stepped back from the emotion of the affair which has become a political issue in Britain in the run-up to a general election.
"Instead they ran into the middle of a storm of English outrage, lost their step and fell over and allowed the DFB (German soccer federation) to be thrown out into the rain," Kicker said.

World governing body FIFA will make the final decision about the event in the year 2000 after receiving bids from across the globe. The Germans believe Europe needs to speak as one voice with just one candidate to have a chance of getting the tournament.
